I can't help but wonder if there's a better sub for this stuff. /v/science is really more about science papers and announcements than this sort of thing.

But, fuck it, I'm here now, so I might as well give this a shot. First, if you want really a lot of information, go to http://contrailscience.com/ where the author lays out a lot of information regarding air traffic control procedures, meteorology, airplane development, etc.

The thing about most of those pictures is that they show either airplanes that have been modified for research, or they show airplanes that are flying in conditions where clouds are already almost forming and the disturbance from the passing airplane finally tips the balance and forces water vapor to come out of the air and form clouds.

First, the research craft. The most common pictures of tanks inside airplane cabins are actually showing test flight equipment for testing how far the center of gravity can move in the plane. If the CG is too far forward, the plane flies poorly, and if the CG is too far back, it crashes. So, to fly safely, we have to know just how many obese passengers can sit in the back end of coach before the CG goes outside the safe range and everybody dies. And that's what those tanks are for. You pump the water around to move the CG and see how the plane flies.

Then there are the airplanes that are covered in nozzles and holes and tubes. If you don't know a whole lot about airplane design, these can look really strange (and I'm not trying to be condescending: I'm a senior in engineering school and I've been into airplanes my whole life, but I still don't understand all the different things about airplane design). The thing is, there are a lot of reasons that airplanes have those things on them. First, every modern airplane has a "pitot tube" that sticks out and senses how much pressure is pushing on the front of the plane. This is how they measure airspeed on production aircraft, but on test aircraft, they often have more than one of these and they'll be covered in holes and sensors to measure all sorts of stuff about the airflow. Second, most modern jets have "Auxiliary Power Units" that are small turbine engines which are used to provide power to the airplane's machinery for various reasons. These can be in a lot of weird places, like way back in the tail or near the main engines. Third, there are fuel dumping ports for if the airplane needs to get lighter in a hurry. Fourth, airborne fuel tankers have more than one way to refuel other airplanes. Most people have seen the booms that stick out into the refueling port on other airplanes, but there are also often wingtip pods that drag a fuel hose on a parachute behind the plane. Fifth... Man, I don't even know. I could go on for a long time listing all the weird things that people have put on airplanes, and I'd never run out. But if you take the time to learn about them (which, granted, can be a lot of time) they almost always have perfectly benign reasons for being there, and the exceptions are always things like weapons systems and cameras on military planes, never chemtrail sprayers.

And then we consider the pictures of clouds. First, remember that clouds form when there is too much water in the air - and how much that is depends on air pressure and temperature - and that water has something it can form a droplet on, like microscopic dust or smoke or something. So that means that changes in temperature can cause clouds, changes in pressure can cause clouds, changes in humidity can cause clouds, and changes in airborne particulates can cause clouds. When an airplane climbs or descends, the air pressure, temperature, and humidity all change as it passes through layers of the atmosphere. Furthermore, jet engines burn a lot of fuel. Like, it's hard to overstate how much they burn. And every bit of that fuel turns into a little water vapor, a little smoke, and a little heat. This changes the humidity, the temperature, and the particulates in the air that an airplane flies through. And then on top of that, airplanes produce huge wingtip vortices that look like big long sushi rolls in the sky. The pressure in the middle of those vortices is lower than outside them, and the jet exhaust tends to get sucked into them, too, so all the changes the jet engine exhaust causes are also in the vortices. (This is also why a plane with four engines still produces two big rolls in its contrail: The rolls don't come from the engines, they come from the wingtips.)

The big thing that people object to when people like me talk about how contrails form is "well, why do some airplanes cause them and others don't? For that matter, why can one airplane seem to turn them off and on?" That's because not every airplane is flying through air where conditions are almost right to form clouds. In a lot of weather situations, you'll see multiple layers of clouds, like for example low stratus and high cirrus. The fact that two separate layers of clouds can possibly exist at one time is proof that there can be multiple layers of air where conditions can be good in some and bad in others, all mixed up. So if you have a picture of two airplanes, and only one is forming contrails, that's not because it's spraying and the other isn't, it's because they're flying at different altitudes where conditions are different. And then when one airplane leaves a contrail in some places and not in others, they're either crossing through multiple layers of air as they climb or descend, or they're skimming the boundary between two air masses and passing repeatedly between air that's good for clouds and air that isn't (This second one isn't great, because it tends to make for a more turbulent ride and pilots try to avoid it when they can.)

I can't explain all of these. I don't have the time. But I hope this gives you a good start.
